articles.title: Taiwan Isn’t Giving Up, It’s Pulling Apart
articles.full_text:
Rising passivity in Taiwan doesn’t mean Taiwanese have given up on resisting. It means the conditions for political action are eroding.
A KMT-led rally on July 20, 2025, urges a “no” vote in the July 26 recalls.
In a recent article for The Diplomat, Mor Sobol offered an even-handed assessment of the debate set off by Simon Shuster’s piece in The Atlantic, which asked whether Taiwan might simply “give up” under growing pressure from China. Sobol argued that both Shuster’s pessimistic answer and his critics’ confident rebuttals rest on thinner evidence than either side recognizes. 
Sobol pointed out that telling a pollster “I would defend Taiwan” is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, and that Taiwan is not a unitary actor. The question worth asking is how the trends in public opinion, military recruitment, defense spending and other metrics move over time, not what any single snapshot shows.
I agree. As a scholar who studies Taiwanese defense attitudes with survey data, I want to add evidence showing why the much-discussed “willingness to fight” has, to some degree, misled outside observers. The problem with polling is not that attitudes can’t be measured. It’s that pollsters keep asking the most superficial question. “Would you fight?” captures a sentiment. What decides whether that sentiment translates into action is whether citizens believe the conditions for sacrifice are in place. Those conditions can be measured, tracked over time, and broken down by group. 
When we do that, the picture is more troubling than either the optimists or the pessimists suggest, though for different reasons.
Citizens never accept the risks of war unconditionally. They take part in what I call a Defense Social Contract, which rests on three pillars, all of them vitally important.
The first pillar is trust in the state. People will sacrifice for a government they believe governs competently and fairly, and for a country they believe has a future worth defending. When citizens feel the state has failed them, its claim to extraordinary sacrifice loses legitimacy.
The second pillar is trust in one another. Defense is a public good, and public goods invite free-riding. I will hold the line only if I believe my neighbors will too. That means the burden must be shared, rather than some Taiwanese being expected to serve while others are exempt. Resistance must also be the common cause of all Taiwanese, not the property of one political camp.
The final pillar is trust that resistance can work. Facing a far more powerful adversary, citizens of a small democracy must believe their own military is capable and that allies will arrive in time. Sacrifice that looks futile turns into fatalism.
If any one pillar gives way, professed willingness to fight stays a sentiment and never becomes action.
All three pillars can be measured. To do so, I used two nationally representative waves of the Taiwan National Security Survey (TNSS), fielded in June 2024 and September 2025, with 2,745 respondents in total. This makes it possible to do what Sobol recommends: track change over time and look inside the aggregate. The timing deserves emphasis. The 2024 survey was fielded about a month after President Lai Ching-te took office. The 2025 survey was fielded about a month after the final round of Taiwan’s Great Recall votes, a national effort to recall all legislators from the Kuomintang (KMT) that ultimately failed.
The TNSS directly asks respondents what they would actually do if China invaded. One option is to “let nature take its course” (shun qi zi ran). That answer is not surrender, and it is not a rejection of Taiwan. It is withdrawal: wait and see. I call it fatalistic passivity. Between the two waves, the share of Taiwanese choosing it rose from about 26 percent to nearly 37 percent.
From 2024 to 2025, the TNSS results showed that all three pillars weakened or came under strain.
On trust in the state, the share of respondents who said the national economy had gotten worse rose from 31 to 48 percent. Negative economic evaluations are strongly associated with passivity, although the association weakens once other factors are taken into account.
The share who doubt Taiwan’s military could defend the island on its own rose from 69 to 74 percent. Confidence in the military and the expectation of U.S. intervention are among the strongest and most consistent predictors of lower passivity across every model. Passivity is highest among those pessimistic on both counts.
Finally, there’s trust in fellow Taiwanese. Respondents who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” are much less likely to opt to “let nature take its course.” Predicted passivity falls from about 36 percent among those who think their compatriots definitely would not resist to about 25 percent among those who think they definitely would.
The most important finding, however, is not the numbers themselves. It’s the breakdown of the survey results along political lines. Among respondents who identified with the KMT, expressions of passivity rose from 22 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025, an 18-point jump. That difference holds after controlling for national identity, unification-independence preferences, confidence in the military, expectations of U.S. assistance, economic evaluations, and demographics. Among Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) identifiers, it rose from 26 to 30.5 percent, a change statistically indistinguishable from zero. The 13.6-point gap between the two trajectories is statistically significant.
I want to stress what this does not mean, because the finding is easy to misread. On its face, it might seem to show that KMT supporters love Taiwan less or are less willing to defend it. That’s not accurate. In 2024, KMT identifiers were actually slightly less fatalistic than DPP identifiers. In other words, at the start of Lai’s presidency, KMT supporters showed no sign of giving up on Taiwan’s defense simply because the DPP had won another term. 
In neither wave is the partisan gap on its own statistically significant. Both surveys took place under a DPP government, with KMT supporters in opposition throughout. The divergence between June 2024 and September 2025 therefore suggests that something changed over those 15 months in how the opposition camp relates to the DPP government. 
Between the two surveys, Taiwan went through more than a year of fierce executive-legislative conflict, ending in the 2025 Great Recall. Advocates framed the campaign to remove 31 KMT legislators as a defense of national security against Chinese infiltration. Opponents saw it as an attempt to overturn an election result. All 31 recall votes failed. The September 2025 survey was fielded weeks later. 
The partisan gap was already there. In both waves of the TNSS, KMT identifiers were about 20 points less likely than DPP identifiers to believe most Taiwanese would resist (roughly 61-63 percent versus 80-82 percent). In both the DPP and the KMT, the share who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” barely moved from 2024 to 2025. A substantial share of the electorate had already lost confidence that the burden would be shared.
But people’s own willingness to act did change, and it fell most among supporters of the KMT, whose political opponents had been presenting national security as a partisan cause.
Survey data cannot prove that any single event caused the shift. But when the language of national security becomes a weapon in domestic political combat, this pattern should come as no surprise. 
My reading is that the problem for Taiwan’s defense is not a lack of will but a lack of unity. It is very hard to ask citizens to risk their lives alongside people they already dislike and distrust in everyday politics, or to sacrifice for a government they see as a political adversary. The TNSS does not directly measure cross-partisan trust, so this interpretation needs further testing. It fits the evidence, though: a society that still sees itself as one nation but is increasingly unsure it can fight as one.
To gauge Taiwan’s willingness to fight, Sobol argued for watching behavior: recruitment, retention, reserve training, and civil defense participation. I strongly agree. I would add three sets of attitudinal indicators that come before this behavior and help explain it.
Do supporters of every party believe that the government asking for sacrifice governs fairly and competently, and that the country has a future?
Do citizens believe the burden is shared? Conscription reform, reserve obligations, and civil defense must be seen as universal, not selective. National security must stop being used against political opponents. Leaders of all parties should stop branding one another as Beijing’s proxies and should negotiate defense budgets and reforms as cross-party agreements.
Are allied signals consistent? Taiwanese must believe they can hold out until help arrives. Mixed messages from Washington or Tokyo damage the very pillar my data identify as most critical. Allies should also engage Taiwan’s major parties evenly, so that outside support is not seen as backing one camp.
These indicators should be broken down by party, age, gender, and region, and tracked across survey waves. If behavior and attitudes move together, across various segments of society, we can trust them more. If the aggregate holds steady while part of society quietly pulls back, we are looking at what I call “fragile resilience.”
articles.summary: Rising passivity in Taiwan doesn’t mean Taiwanese have given up on resisting. It means the conditions for political action are eroding.

articles.title: ‘Xi, You’re Not Welcome’: As Trump Hosts China’s Leader, Thousands Protest in Washington
articles.full_text:
Over 3,000 Tibetans, Chinese dissidents, Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and other groups joined protests during Xi’s state visit, calling for human rights and political freedom.
Tibetan protesters hold Tibetan national flags and banners during a demonstration outside the Chinese Embassy against Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., on Sep. 24, 2026. The protesters called for a Free Tibet.
On September 24, more than 3,000 Tibetans gathered in Washington to protest Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House, in what organizers described as the largest-ever Tibetan rally in North America. The rally was organized by Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) and supported by other Tibetan activist organizations.
The protesters came with demands that they said should be part of the China-U.S. relationship: that Trump raise human rights with Xi, that China release political and religious prisoners, and that Tibetans be allowed to preserve their language and culture. The group also demanded the repeal of China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which took effect in July and promotes what Beijing calls a shared sense of identity among China’s 56 ethnic groups. Tibetan activists say the law further advances Beijing’s efforts to assimilate Tibetans into Chinese identity. Chinese authorities say the law protects minority rights while promoting ethnic unity.
“Human rights should not be left outside of their talks,” said Tencho Gyatso, president of the International Campaign for Tibet. “The Tibetans, the Uyghurs, the Hong Kongers, the Taiwanese, we want to make sure our voices are also heard there.”
The demonstration unfolded as Xi made his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade. U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed him to the White House for talks that touched on AI, trade, and other issues, while the two governments were also dealing with disputes over Taiwan, Iran and rare earths. Trump hosted Xi at a state dinner on the evening of September 24.
Outside, Tibetan protesters marched through the capital carrying Tibetan flags and signs reading “Xi Jinping is guilty of genocide” and “Tibet was never a part of China.” By the end of the day, the demonstration had expanded into a coalition that included Uyghur, Southern Mongolian, Chinese democracy, Taiwanese, Burmese, Falun Gong, and Chinese Christian groups, all people that have suffered under the Chinese Communist Party.
The rally began at about 9 a.m. outside the Chinese Embassy, where protesters gathered before marching toward the U.S. Capitol. Police were deployed around the demonstration as the crowd assembled. The protesters then moved through Washington, with Connecticut Avenue closed to accommodate the march. The crowd passed through Dupont Circle before arriving at the Capitol, where several speakers addressed the demonstrators.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, joined the rally. McGovern called for human rights to be included in Trump’s discussions with Xi.
“No Xi in D.C. without human rights,” McGovern told the crowd.
He also criticized Republican lawmakers, who he said had declined to join efforts urging the administration to press China on human rights. “Are they afraid of Donald Trump? Are they afraid he’ll be offended if they ask him to ask Xi to release prisoners of conscience?” McGovern said.
Pelosi also spoke in support of the protesters, calling attention to human rights in Tibet and urging the release of prisoners of conscience.
For many Tibetan protesters, Thursday’s demonstration was also shaped by the death of Lobga Rangzen, a longtime Tibetan independence activist who died after self-immolating outside the United Nations in New York on July 2. Rangzen, 52, had called for Tibetan independence and unity in a final message before setting himself on fire.
Jigme Ugen, president of the Tibetan National Congress, said the size of the demonstration showed that the Tibetan independence movement remained active.
“This is the biggest gathering, as such, to not just protest Xi Jinping, but also to tell the world and the U.S. government that the Tibetan movement, and the call for Tibetan independence, is still very much alive,” Ugen said. 
Tsering Chomphel, president of the Tibetan Youth Congress, who traveled from India for the protest, said people had come from New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago, Vermont, and Toronto. “This is the first-ever mass gathering in North America. Whenever Xi Jinping or a Chinese delegation visits, TYC will be there to make sure our voices are heard.”
Seventeen Tibetans had set off on foot from the United Nations headquarters in New York on September 17, walking through Philadelphia before reaching Washington on the evening of September 23 – the same day Xi arrived. Rangzen Dolkar, one of the walkers, said the journey was meant to raise awareness about Tibet and Pawo Lobga Rangzen’s death. 
Pawo is an honorary title given to any individual who has sacrificed their lives through self-immolation to bring attention to Tibet’s situation. 
“I am a mother of two kids, and I left my kids home. We all took off from work and left on this journey,” she said. “People stop us on the way and ask us what we’re doing because they see the flag. It gives us an opportunity to speak about Tibet and what Pawo Lobga Rangzen sacrificed his life for.”
After the rally at the Capitol, the protestors marched to Franklin Park, half a mile from the White House, where speakers from the Uyghur, Taiwanese, Burmese, and Hong Kong communities addressed the crowd. 
Misran Dolan, president of the Uyghur American Association, framed the gathering as a common demand for political and religious freedom. “Free the Uyghurs. Free the Tibetans. Keep Taiwan free. Keep Hong Kong free. Keep China free,” Dolan told the crowd.
“All of us here have moved away from our homelands,” he said. “And now we’re here in the United States … to exercise those rights – freedom of speech, freedom of expression, freedom of religion.” About 200 members of the Uyghur community attended, according to Dolan.
The gathering also included Chinese democracy activists. About 50 members of the Democratic Party of China traveled from Los Angeles, according to Zheng Zhou, a member of the group.
“We want Xi Jinping to stop persecuting people. We want him to free Jimmy Lai, Ding Jiaxi,” said Zhou. Lai, the billionaire founder of Apple Daily, Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy newspaper, and a vocal critic of the Chinese Communist Party was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier this February after being convicted of conspiracy to commit sedition and collusion with foreign forces. Marco Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state, had urged the CCP to grant him humanitarian parole calling the sentence unjust and tragic, 
Daniel Zhou, a Chinese Christian affiliated with an underground church – churches that operate outside China’s state-controlled religious system and whose members can face detention and other restrictions from authorities – spoke about the persecution of Christians in China.
“Our church leaders have to stay in Chinese jails, leaving their families praying and crying at home, just because they wanted to practice their religion peacefully in China,” Zhou said.
Cynthia Sun, a senior researcher at the Falun Dafa Information Center, said her friends from the United States had family members killed in Chinese prison through forced organ harvesting. “When they went to see their dead parents at the mortuary, their bodies were split open, there were stitches, and they were missing a heart or a kidney,” she said. 
Falun Gong is a spiritual practice that emerged in China in the 1990s and was banned by Chinese authorities in 1999. The Chinese government has been accused of forcibly harvesting organs from imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners. In 2019, the China Tribunal, an independent people’s tribunal, concluded that forced organ harvesting has occurred in China on a significant scale and that Falun Gong practitioners were likely the main source of organs. 
Sun described the persecution of Falun Gong practitioners as something that had followed her throughout her life. 
“I was born in July 1999, the month and year that the persecution began,” she said. “When I graduated high school, I thought the persecution would end by the time I got to college. But now I’m in grad school. I’m engaged, I’m getting married, and the persecution is still going on.”
articles.summary: Over 3,000 Tibetans, Chinese dissidents, Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and other groups joined protests during Xi’s state visit, calling for human rights and political freedom.

The visit’s outcomes are thin: a small extension of the trade truce and two pandas.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Punitive Gamble in Afghanistan: An Open War With No End in Sight
articles.full_text:
The Afghan Taliban have little incentive to accede to Islamabad’s demands.
In the early hours of September 24, Pakistan carried out air and drone strikes on ten locations inside Afghanistan. Subsequently, Afghan media identified Kandahar – where the Taliban’s supreme leader (Amir-al-Mu’minin) Hibatullah Akhundzada is based – as well as Khost and Paktia as the provinces targeted. A few hours later, Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted on social media that the strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate” and were “strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan.” “Attempted attacks” was a reference to earlier Pakistani claims that it had shot down ten rudimentary drones launched from inside Afghanistan that entered Pakistani territory with a “soft kill” approach. 
Two days earlier, on September 21, Pakistani air strikes on Kunar and Paktika provinces killed three civilians – a man, a woman, and a girl – in Kunar’s Nurgal district. Islamabad claimed to have killed 28 militants in the attack. The civilian casualties, which were confirmed by UNAMA, saw Afghan protesters hitting the streets in Kabul and elsewhere. 
This Pakistani strike was in response to an attack on a police compound in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat, killing at least 16 police officers on September 18. On that day a vehicle-borne explosive device breached the police compound during Friday prayers. This was followed by an armed assault by militants. The attack was claimed by the Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), an alliance led by the Hafiz Gul Bahadar (HGB) group, which shares close linkages with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Pakistani authorities identified one of the attackers as an Afghan national. 
Pakistan has carried out air and drone strikes inside Afghanistan on at least 15 occasions between October 2025 and September 2026. Private estimates suggest that more than 1,100 civilians have been killed or injured by cross-border violence in Afghanistan this year. An attack on a drug rehabilitation center in Kabul in May killed 269 people, leading to calls for the attack to be investigated as a war crime.  
Inside Pakistan, the death toll of civilians and security forces in terrorism-related incidents in 2026 so far is close to 1,700. Of these, 545 have taken place in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the TTP and the IMP operate.
Pakistani claims that Afghan soil is being used by the TTP and the IMP are supported by periodic reports from the U.N. monitoring committee, including one released in August 2026. The report unequivocally said that the Afghan Taliban “continued their support” to the TTP. The Afghan Taliban has responded to such assertions by repeated public denials. 
Behind the scenes, however, the Afghan Taliban may have tried to restrain the TTP. The U.N. report mentioned that the Afghan Taliban authorities have “relocated approximately 2,000 TTP fighters and families from the Pakistani border to further inside Afghanistan.” Akhundzada has reportedly “warned the TTP leadership through back‑channel communications to halt attacks targeting Pakistan or risk losing the Taliban’s support,” it added. It is unclear if any attempt was made to reign in the IMP as well.  
While efforts to control the TTP may not have worked completely, according to data by ACLED, “HGB and IMP’s activities have less than halved since the latest outbreak of hostilities between Afghanistan and Pakistan in late February, compared with the immediately preceding period.” 
On February 27, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil-Haq (Righteous Fury) against the Taliban in Afghanistan, marking the first such attack on its former ally and protégé. On that occasion, “unprovoked firing” from across the border by the Taliban was cited as the reason. Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif declared, “Now it is open war between us.”
Given the levels of violence the TTP and the IMP continued to perpetrate inside Pakistan, the country is facing a classic case of strategic blowback. More importantly, the sense of impunity with which Islamabad has repeatedly carried out its attacks in Afghanistan, despite their low efficacy, indicates serious lacunae in Pakistan’s counterterrorism strategy. Most of these attacks have led to angry statements by Taliban officials, vows of retaliation, and incidents of cross-border firing by Taliban soldiers but little else.    
In addition to reining in the TTP and IMP, Pakistan seems to be pursuing a larger strategic objective of finding its lost leverage in Kabul. In Islamabad’s view, its former ally has gone rogue and demonstrating coercive power, along with providing support to the anti-Taliban resistance fronts, is the only path forward. A weak and client state in Afghanistan is the end state Pakistani establishment has pursued for decades. 
During the days of the previous Afghan Republic, the HGB largely spared the Pakistani state and instead focused its fight on American and NATO forces in Afghanistan. Post-August 2021, backed by al-Qaida, the HGB has grown to be a prominent face of jihadist insurgency against Islamabad. It is numerically smaller than the TTP, but that hasn’t stopped it from carrying out some of the more complex attacks on security installations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. 
Therefore, eliminating the IMP threat, if not the far larger TTP, will potentially address the blowback Islamabad is currently receiving for its past policies. Similarly, repeated attacks including some directed at the Taliban regime itself, could possibly lead to internal ruptures within the faction-ridden Islamic Emirate and embolden the small pro-Pakistan elements within it. 
That, however, is much easier said than done. Despite reports of factionalism and internal differences within the Kandahar (Rahbari shura or the leadership council) and Kabul (administrative) shuras of the Taliban, the Rahbari shura functioning under the strict Islamic edicts of the Supreme leader, still retains control and uncontested legitimacy. Moreover, each attack by Pakistan so far has further raised anti-Pakistan sentiment inside Afghanistan. It could embolden the Afghan Taliban as well, who have little incentive to accede to Islamabad’s demands. The ethno-nationalist Taliban regime with strong Pushtun identity across the contested Durand Line could raise its head of Pushtun nationalism once again. 
The Taliban seem to have learnt from their former sponsor’s playbook the art of cultivating strategic assets and using them as leverage. Attempting to bomb them into submission could be a myopic and counterproductive strategy if there are any lessons learned from the last two decades of American intervention in Afghanistan.

articles.title: Trump-Xi Summit: Heavy of Vibes, Light on Substance
articles.full_text:
Good feelings were on display, but there was no real movement on the many areas of friction.
U.S. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping of China arrive via the Cross Hall to a State Arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House, Sep.24, 2026.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping held a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump on September 24, Trump made sure Xi knew how he felt. The U.S. leader expressed no fewer than three times in the first minute of their joint remarks that it was his “honor” – or even “great honor” – to host Xi. 
The “honor,” apparently was all Trump’s. Xi made no similar expression of feeling “honored” to be hosted by the U.S. president, simply saying he was “glad” to be in Washington. 
That set the tone for a meeting that was long on symbolism but short on substance. Trump was eager to impress; Xi was all business.
Trump was reportedly keen to match the lavish hosting he received during his visit to Beijing in May. As Xi pointed out at the state dinner in Washington, it’s “unprecedented” for the Chinese and American presidents to exchange state visits in such a short period of time. 
“Today, President Trump and I had sincere and in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues,” Xi said. “This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and provided new strategic guidance for China-U.S. relations.”
“The constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability” is Beijing’s new mantra for the relationship – and the first that China has successfully gotten Washington to buy into. The basic gist is that China and the United States will continue to compete – something Beijing has finally admitted is happening, after years of studiously denying any rivalry – but keep their competition “within bounds.” 
Other than agreeing, in principle, not to let their competition spill into conflict, though, it wasn’t immediately clear what “common understandings” were reached at the summit. No major breakthroughs were expected, and that turned out to be accurate.
The biggest deliverable was an agreement – actually reached before the summit, during China-U.S. economic talks on September 20 – to extend their trade truce through January 10. The original deal, reached at the first Trump-Xi summit in Busan, South Korea in October 2025, saw the U.S. lower tariffs on Chinese goods, while Chinese agreed to pause enforcement of export controls on certain critical minerals. The deal was only good for a year initially, and was set to expire in November. 
Many experts had predicted an extension was in the offing – if that hadn’t been the case, it was suggested that there wouldn’t have been much reason for Trump and Xi to meet at all. But the short length of the extension – just two extra months – was a bit of a surprise. Bessent mentioned that China needed to make good on its promises, suggesting that the deal could be extended again if Washington is satisfied with what it sees. Or it could be eventually scrapped. 
China, meanwhile, hasn’t confirmed even that limited extension. The official readout from the Chinese Foreign Ministry said a “new joint arrangement” had been reached in economic and trade discussions, but did not elaborate on what that deal was. 
To recap: the biggest practical impact of the Trump-Xi summit was a possible agreement to slightly extend a pause – not a cancellation – on the worst of the trade war. Oh, and two more pandas for the Atlanta Zoo. That about sums up the fruits of the fragile truce currently in place between China and the United States.
If the outcome on trade was a mixed bag, other areas were even murkier. There was much focus on artificial intelligence (AI) prior to the summit, especially as U.S. AI companies themselves have begun raising safety concerns. There had been suggestions that the U.S. and China could unveil an “AI safety mechanism” that would see both sides notify the other of concerning incidents. 
Trump, however, has consistently rejected any calls for additional oversight of AI – precisely because he wants the United States to go full speed ahead in the race against China. In a Truth Social post, prior to the summit, Trump stated that AI (which he has started referring to as “super intelligence”) “will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.”
Xi, however, was more cautious on AI, referencing the need to “jointly prevented the misuse and abuse of AI,” and emphasizing that “AI must be kept under human control.” But, like Trump, his primary concern was the AI race and preventing the U.S. from “guarding against” China’s AI development through export controls and other restrictions. As James Wang noted in a recent analysis for The Diplomat, Beijing is well aware of Washington’s tendency to frame restrictions on Chinese technology as safety measures. 
As expected, Xi also brought up Taiwan. He explicitly asked “the U.S. side” to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence.’” Much reporting ahead of the summit held that Xi was hoping to get Trump to explicitly say that the U.S. “opposes Taiwan independence.” The usual phrasing is that the U.S. “does not support Taiwan independence.” For China, an outright expression of opposition would be a key win – especially because Beijing purposefully conflates Taiwan’s ruling party and president with “Taiwan independence forces.”  
Beijing is also hoping to extend the current “pause” on U.S. arms sales to Taiwan to a de facto moratorium – something it’s tried to do in the past, but without success. Whenever a U.S. administration signals openness to scaling back arms sales to please China, Beijing ups the pressure. 
Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, called the current period the “fourth Taiwan arms sale freeze,” following “two under former President George W. Bush from 2005-2007 and 2007-2008, and one under former President Barack Obama from 2011-2015.” In all these cases, Hammond-Chambers argued, the “freeze” did nothing more than embolden Beijing.
“The Trump Administration has let the fox in the henhouse. Telegraphing sensitivity to the Chinese position on Taiwan this past spring, Trump has empowered China to affect his decisions [on arms sales],” Hammond-Chambers wrote in a media release.
There’s been no movement on the arms sale, which has been on hold since before the May summit. 
As with the Trump-Xi summit in May, this time there was another brief reference to an exchange of views “on major international and regional issues including the situation in the Middle East, the Ukraine crisis and the Korean Peninsula.” There was, however, no suggestion of any agreement or alignment on those issues – unlike after the May summit, when Trump got Xi to say that China opposes Iran’s development of nuclear weapons and supports “the free flow of energy” through the Strait of Hormuz.
If the actual substance showed little sign of convergence, you’d never know it from the optics. Trump lauded his “truly great friendship” with Xi and showed special deference to the Chinese president, including personally meeting him on the tarmac upon Xi’s arrival in the United States. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump also arranged an opulent welcome ceremony, featuring musical performances and drills by 479 military personnel and ending with a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 fighter jets. 
After the summit proper came the state dinner attended by a who’s who list of top American businesspeople: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and Elon Musk of Tesla, X, and SpaceX. 
Notably, though, Xi did not bring his own entourage of business leaders – a marked contrast with Trump’s visit to Beijing, when he included top CEOs in his delegation. Speaking to the New York Times, Emily Kilcrease of the Center for a New American Security called the absence of Chinese business leaders “a rather depressing marks of how bad the relationship has gotten.” 
Overall, the summit left the impression of a stable, positive relationship, but there was little to back up that sentiment. Trump claimed that he and Xi had “made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries” – including the “unbelievably successful” Board of Trade, which hasn’t actually even launched yet – but as always, there were no specifics.
Xi’s positive comments, meanwhile, were mostly forward-looking. “[T]hrough candid, in-depth, and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” he said – an aspiration, not an accomplishment.
Xi also emphasize the parallels between the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” and Trump’s “make America great again” slogan, which he argued can “be mutually reinforcing.” Xi continued: “Our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses.”
It was a somewhat odd way of trying to cast competition as “win-win.” I don’t know what races Xi has been watching, but generally those have a winner as well – and multiple losers. 
Given the shallow nature of the current era of good feelings in China-U.S. relations, it’s telling that the trade truce was extended only until January 10 – just long enough to keep relations steady through the APEC summit (to be held in Shenzhen, China from November 18-19) and the G20 summit (Miami, the United States, December 14-15). Assuming Trump and Xi attend both events, that could set up two additional summits, for a total of four in 2026 alone.
articles.summary: Good feelings were on display, but there was no real movement on the many areas of friction.

articles.title: The Promises the Afghanistan War Left Behind
articles.full_text:
Five years after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, the relationships built over 20 years of war still matter.
U.S. Air Force loadmasters and pilots assigned to the 816th Expeditionary Airlift Squadron, load passengers aboard a U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster III in support of the Afghanistan evacuation at Hamid Karzai International Airport (HKIA), Afghanistan, Aug. 24, 2021.
“It felt almost like you were playing God with their life at that moment,” recalled Joe Laude, executive director of the Operation Allies Refuge Foundation (OAR),  reflecting on the final days of the U.S. evacuation from Kabul. A Marine machine-gunner with Echo Company, 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines who served at Abbey Gate during the evacuation in August 2021, Laude witnessed firsthand the impossible choices facing Americans as approximately 123,000 people were evacuated and thousands of Afghans sought a way out.  
Every decision – to let someone through the gate, to turn someone away – carried life-altering consequences. When the last U.S. aircraft departed Kabul on August 30, 2021, those decisions lingered. For people like Laude, the uncertainties remained: Who could he have helped? Who was left behind? And what did it mean to feel responsible for people he could not protect? 
Psychologists describe these experiences as moral injury, the psychological and ethical harm that occurs when individuals witness, participate in, or are unable to prevent actions that violate their deeply held moral beliefs and values. In the aftermath of the United States’ 20-year war  in Afghanistan, that injury can take the form of responsibility, helplessness, perceived betrayal, and the painful belief that a promise was left unfulfilled. 
For two decades, Americans and Afghans worked shoulder to shoulder in pursuit of a shared mission. Afghan interpreters, journalists, civil society leaders, educators, and security personnel risked their lives alongside American soldiers, diplomats, and aid workers. These relationships were often more than professional. They were built through years of shared danger, trust, friendship, and a belief that those who had stood beside one another would be protected if the situation deteriorated. However, with the Taliban’s return in August 2021, much of that shared progress disappeared almost overnight.
Lida Kharooti Sayeed, who served as a judge on Afghanistan’s Anti-Corruption Serious Crimes Court for 13 years before the Taliban returned to power, remembers with gratitude the Americans who tried to help her and others like her. 
“I do not blame the individuals who tried to help us,” she said. “Many of them showed kindness and compassion where people were frightened and uncertain about their future. Their efforts meant a great deal to Afghan people like me.”  
Sayeed’s gratitude complicates an easy narrative of American failure. The people who formed these relationships fought on the same side of a war. They were people who trusted one another. 
That trust also made the withdrawal so difficult for those who were unable to protect the people they had worked beside. Laude describes the guilt he felt: “I had betrayed the Afghan community, even though it was ultimately our leadership’s decision that led to what happened.”
That distinction did not necessarily ease the burden. Knowing that institutions and leaders made the ultimate decisions did not erase the responsibility he felt toward the Afghans who were calling, asking for help, and waiting for a way out. 
Helping Afghan allies became a way to channel that unresolved feeling into action. Through OAR, Laude has turned his experience in Kabul into work supporting veterans struggling with moral injury through peer support, humanitarian service, research, and advocacy.  
Laude acknowledged that staying busy also meant putting his own emotions aside. “Part of what I did was try to mask the emotional side of this situation through work. That’s why I started OAR. I tried to take away from my own healing and help other people.”
For some, continuing to serve Afghan partners may be a form of moral repair – not an attempt to pretend the past can be fixed, but a decision to remain accountable to the values and friendships that still matter. 
For Afghan partners left behind, the story did not end with the evacuation. Families remain separated, immigration cases stretch on, and careers and lives are disrupted. 
Sayeed is still rebuilding the life she lost. She’s now a visiting scholar and researcher at the William & Mary Law School. 
“We survived very difficult days, but surviving was only the beginning,” she said. “We are still trying to rebuild our lives, support our families, continue our education, and find meaningful opportunities.”
Five years later, Afghanistan is still often discussed in terms of the political failures surrounding the withdrawal. Those debates are important, but they do not capture everything that remained after the last plane left Kabul. What happens to the relationships built during 20 years of war when the war itself is over? Can there be closure? 
For some, the answer has been to keep showing up. “That closure isn’t necessarily going to come through the leadership that betrayed you. Instead, I think it comes through relationships at the grassroots level,” Laude said.
For Laude, those relationships offer more than a path toward closure. They shape how he answers a harder question about the war itself: whether the years of service, sacrifice, and relationships built along the way ultimately mattered. 
“One of the most important long-term psychological questions is whether any of it mattered,” Laude said. “I believe it does matter.”
What endures, five years later, is not only the memory of the withdrawal, but the relationships and obligations it could not erase. The war may have ended, but for those who believed they were responsible for one another, the question of what was owed did not end with it.

articles.title: What’s Behind Australia’s New $42 Million in Assistance to Ukraine?
articles.full_text:
Canberra’s desire to learn from Kyiv is a sign of enormous respect and its pledge to ongoing support an expression of Australia’s support for the Ukrainian cause.
Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York this week. Out of that meeting came a new bilateral security agreement, unlocking a further US$42 million in Australian assistance to Ukraine – split between Australian Defense Force (ADF) equipment, Ukraine’s Energy Support Fund, and humanitarian assistance. This brings Australia’s total contribution to almost US$1.4 billion. 
Ukraine is obviously far away from Australia’s immediate security concerns in the Indo-Pacific, but Canberra’s support for the country is driven principally by its interest in preventing territorial conquest from becoming an accepted instrument of international relations. As a geographically isolated country with considerable economic interests beyond its immediate region, Australia depends on international rules that constrain the use of force. Canberra understands that allowing this principle to be undermined in Europe would weaken its application elsewhere, including in the Indo-Pacific. Alongside this is the position that smaller and middle-sized countries should retain the freedom to make their own security and diplomatic decisions.
Alongside its assistance package, Australia will also join the United Kingdom and Norway-led Maritime Capability Coalition which is helping Ukraine develop its naval capabilities. Yet what is most interesting about the new security agreement with Ukraine is not so much the assistance that Australia can provide Ukraine, but what Australia can learn from Ukraine. 
Over the past four years, Ukraine has been forced into one of the more consequential live experiments in modern warfare. It has had to develop systems and capabilities that can counter a larger and more well-equipped military force with cunning and creativity. The most visible product of this has been in unmanned systems. Ukraine’s naval drone program, epitomized by the Magura platform, has proved to be a relatively inexpensive, but high impact weapons program adaptable to multiple roles, from attacking warships and aircraft, to striking the industrial infrastructure inside Russia that funds its invading force. 
What makes this experience important and valuable to Australia is not just the technology itself, but what it can learn from how quickly Ukraine has been able to develop and adapt its capabilities. Ukraine has significantly shortened the gap between identifying a battlefield need, developing a solution, and putting it into action. Its defense-tech sector operates more like a startup than a traditional defense industry, as it is constantly adapting and replacing systems as Russia responds. The key lesson is that in a rapidly changing battlefield, the ability to adapt faster than the enemy can be more important than having the most advanced individual systems.
Australia still relies heavily on a small number of highly capable and expensive defense platforms. Yet it is coming to the realization that in a modern warfare scenario, these may not be as impactful as necessary. It is this realization that has driven an element of the new security agreement with Ukraine to deepen cooperation on uncrewed systems. Albanese and Zelenskyy committed the two countries to explore joint production of drones and similar defense technologies. 
Of course, Australia’s own desire to develop autonomous systems predates this week’s agreement. Australia’s flagship Ghost Shark autonomous undersea vehicle is considered one of the more advanced technologies in the maritime space. Australia is not a novice here, but what it is trying to do is fuse the systems it has been working on with the capabilities that Ukraine has developed within an ever-evolving combat zone. The technology has to match the real world practicalities to be useful. 
The Indo-Pacific relevance is what concerns Australia the most. China has been closely observing how Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has unfolded and how Ukraine’s defense of itself could be replicated by Taiwan. The potential for conflict over Taiwan remains the most pressing concern in Australia’s defense planning. Australia is heavily reliant on the sea lines of communication to northeast Asia, making deterrence a vital national interest. Ukraine’s innovative resistance may prove to be a powerful deterrence to any Chinese invasion plans. 
Yet it would be wrong to read this new security agreement with Ukraine purely as one of Australia’s strategic self-interest. Canberra’s support for Ukraine also comes from a straightforward belief that Russia’s invasion is wrong, and helping Ukraine is the right thing to do. Australia’s desire to learn from Ukraine is a sign of enormous respect, and that cooperation in advancing peace is central to any good friendship.

articles.title: Bangladesh’s Youth-led NCP Struggles for an Independent Identity in Jamaat’s Shadow
articles.full_text:
As part of a Jamaat-led alliance, the NCP secured a place in parliament. However, it needs to prove it is an independent force.
Leaders of the National Citizen Party at the launching ceremony of the party on Feb. 28, 2025, at Manik Mia Avenue in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
On September 19, National Citizen Party (NCP) convener Nahid Islam sharply criticized Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. Rahman would eventually have to choose how to leave power, he said. “He must decide whether he will flee the country by helicopter or resign with dignity.”
Nahid was not speaking at an NCP rally. He was addressing a long march organized by the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI)-led 11-party opposition alliance to press a seven-point demand, including implementation of the February referendum verdict, action on rising prices, the energy and fertilizer crisis, deteriorating law and order, and corruption. JI chief Shafiqur Rahman spoke at the same gathering.
This has become a familiar picture in Bangladesh, where NCP routinely joins JI in long marches, alliance meetings and parliamentary protests.
The NCP emerged from the student protests that brought down the Awami League government in August 2024. For a party that entered politics promising a new political alternative, this raises a basic question. What still separates NCP from JI?
NCP says the relationship is strategic, not ideological. But less than two years after emerging from the student-led uprising, the party is struggling to show voters what still makes it politically distinct.
When NCP was launched in February 2025, it carried a heavy political promise. Its leaders had come directly from the student movement that helped bring down Sheikh Hasina’s authoritarian rule. Many were young, had never held party office, and spoke about building a political system different from the one Bangladesh had known for decades.
At its launch, NCP called for a new constitution and a “Second Republic.” It promised democratic institutions, an end to corruption and nepotism, and politics based on equality and representation. Thousands attended the launch in Dhaka. The party presented itself as a centrist force and an alternative to the older parties that had dominated Bangladesh.
Less than two years later, NCP is in parliament. But how it arrived there has created a more difficult question. Can it still convince voters that it represents something genuinely new?
The turning point came before the February 2026 national election, when NCP joined an electoral alliance led by JI.
For a new party without a strong nationwide organization, the calculation was understandable. Elections in Bangladesh require candidates, polling agents, local networks, money and organization across hundreds of constituencies. NCP had enthusiasm and recognizable leaders, but it did not have the machinery of an established party.
But JI’s history made the NCP’s choice contentious. The party had sided with Pakistan against Bangladesh’s independence in 1971, and some of its leaders and members had collaborated with Pakistani forces during the genocide. So, the deal came with a political cost.
Before coming to an agreement with JI, the NCP held seat-sharing talks with the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), while also considering a separate third alliance. NCP reportedly sought at least 20 seats from the BNP, but the party was willing to offer it only around six or seven, with some NCP leaders saying the final number could fall to three.
JI, meanwhile, was prepared to offer around 30 constituencies. For a new party still struggling to build a nationwide organization, the JI deal offered a much clearer path into parliament.
However, in the JI-led alliance, JI received by far the largest share. According to media reports, the decision caused serious resistance inside the NCP. At least 30 senior members either resigned or publicly opposed the alliance. Tasnim Jara, one of the party’s best known figures, left the NCP before the election.
By the NCP’s first anniversary in February, at least 60 leaders and activists had resigned from the party during its first year. Not all left over JI, but the electoral alliance became the clearest public sign of an internal disagreement over what NCP was supposed to become.
NCP leaders have consistently rejected the idea that this means ideological integration with JI. In a March 2026 interview with The Diplomat, Chief Coordinator of NCP Nasiruddin Patwary said NCP had wanted to work with the BNP. But disagreements over reform and electoral realities pushed the party toward JI. He said JI’s religious ideology was not NCP’s position and argued that if the two parties believed in the same politics, NCP would have simply joined JI.
In the February election, NCP won only six parliamentary seats. JI won 68 while the 11-party coalition won a total of 77 seats among 300.
For a party less than a year old, six MPs cannot simply be dismissed as failure.
But the numbers also show the limits of NCP’s rise. It had emerged from a national uprising and once hoped to compete across Bangladesh. Instead, it entered parliament after contesting in only a small part of the country under a seat-sharing arrangement dominated by JI.
Some young Bangladeshis saw the alliance as a retreat from the politics NCP had originally promised. The party also faced more basic problems. It lacked the resources, organization and local structure enjoyed by older parties.
The bigger challenge is what happened after the election. The partnership with JI did not end when voting ended. JI chief Shafiqur Rahman became leader of the opposition. NCP convener Nahid Islam became opposition chief whip. The two parties remained together in the opposition bloc.
Their cooperation has continued well beyond parliament.
This creates challenges for its political identity. NCP says it is a separate party. That is true institutionally. But voters do not judge political identity only through party constitutions or official statements. They also see who shares platforms, who coordinates parliamentary action and who campaigns together on the streets.
The more NCP operates within the JI-led bloc, the harder it may become to explain what makes NCP politically distinct from the alliance around it.
Other controversies have also hurt the NCP’s image. Spokesperson Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain, a former interim government adviser, is under investigation by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) over allegations, including abuse of power and accumulation of illegal wealth. The ACC has said the allegations are not yet proven, while Asif has rejected them.
NCP’s student wing Jatiya Chhatra Shakti (JCS) has also faced scrutiny. In March, a Dhaka University student accused JCS activists of beating him. In August, its activists were involved in a clash with Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, BNP’s student wing, and Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir, JI’s student wing, at Jagannath University in Dhaka that left at least 70 people injured.
NCP had promised a different kind of politics. Incidents like these raise questions about how different it really is.
NCP has also struggled to show what is genuinely new about its politics. Much of its agenda still centers on constitutional reform, criticism of India, and street programs that often take place alongside JI. The two parties frequently use similar language about sovereignty, foreign influence, and reform.
articles.summary: As part of a Jamaat-led alliance, the NCP secured a place in parliament. However, it needs to prove it is an independent force.

articles.title: Thailand’s Independent Institutions Have Lost All Credibility
articles.full_text:
The institutions created by the “People’s Constitution” of 1997 have become tools of the country’s political and economic elite.
Earlier last week, Thailand’s Election Commission (EC) announced its long-awaited decision on whether to refer allegations of collusion in the manipulation of the 2024 Senate election to the courts. The referrals were the product of a joint investigative panel formed by the EC and the Department of Special Investigation in July 2026. That recommendation produced 229 potential referrals to the Supreme Court. The question of whether the EC would refer all 229 individuals to the authorities for trial was closely watched – and posed a stiff test of political transparency and accountability in Thailand.
However, in investigating whether powerful political interests, including executives of the ruling Bhumjaithai Party, members of parliament, cabinet ministers, and local political officials, conspired in the election, the EC decided to take the middle road and refer just 77, none of whom were political party executives, House MPs, or reserve senators. The rationale, the EC claimed, was based on the evidence against each individual, their direct conduct in the scheme, and verification of paper or financial records.
The Senate collusion case centers on claims of fraud, rigged voting, and coordinated manipulation in the 2024 Senate election. Senators were chosen through a multi-round system where candidates voted among themselves rather than through a public ballot, which arguably strengthened allegations of impropriety and collusion by election observers. Investigations also centered on hotel stays, travel costs, and cash to secure compliance in the scheme, with many involved linked directly to Bhumjaithai, giving rise to the dubious “Blue Senate” moniker.
The EC’s decision was not the least bit surprising, as the body has long been accused of being politically compromised. Narong Klunwarin, the chair of the EC, and other members of the Commission were a key part of the regulatory process that further exacerbated Thailand’s flawed electoral processes. Narong Rakroi, who lost a 4-3 decision to become chair in November of 2025, allegedly had the support of the so-called “blue” bloc of Bhumjaithai politicians, a slate that ended up being caught in the Senate collusion investigation. Under Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha’s administration and since, the EC had ample opportunities to rule in a transparent fashion, but did not. During the 2019 election, it failed to investigate widespread allegations of fraud; it quickly intervened that same year in the eventual dissolution of the Thaksin-backed Thai Raksa Chart party, and also requested the dismissal of the Move Forward Party in 2024 on grounds that it violated Thailand’s lese-majeste laws.
And while this perceived dereliction of duty by the EC currently dominates headlines, the dilemma for a host of independent institutions in Thailand remains the same, as they share the same reputation for malfeasance, the same deficiencies in public trust, and compromised independence due to documented political connections and authoritarian appointments. The “People’s Constitution” of 1997 was supposed to usher in a new era of constitutionalism, with the EC, the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), and the Constitutional Court created by this semi-democratic legislative act.
The current political climate was created by consecutive authoritarian interventions by military and royalist elites, which slowly eroded what remains of institutional independence, beginning with the 2006 coup, which led to the creation of the 2007 Constitution. This was then replaced by the 2014 Interim Constitution after the May 2014 military coup, which in turn was replaced by the 2017 Constitution that was put to a referendum in February 2016. Each intervention saw the mutation of these independent institutions into their current, politically compromised states.
The NACC has also fallen far, rather quickly. During the Yingluck Shinawatra government (2011-2014), the NACC seized on petitions by the opposition to bring charges of political corruption for the government’s rice pledging scheme. While the program had serious flaws, the NACC worked suspiciously quickly, moving to file formal charges within three weeks. Another Pheu Thai Party government was brought down by the same NACC playbook. With Prayut using his Article 44 powers under the old interim Constitution, he stacked the NACC with loyalists, extending then-NACC President Panthep Klanarongran, while Suchart Trakulkasemsuk, the current president of the NACC, was selected by the junta-controlled Senate in 2020. The political connections of junta-era officials have led to prison sentences, as was the case for Supa Piyajitti, the NACC commissioner who was instrumental in the rice pledging investigation.
Last, but certainly not least, is the Constitutional Court. The Court is loathed in democratic circles for its dissolution of both the Future Forward and Move Forward parties, including a 10-year ban from politics on the charismatic Pita Limjaroenrat, the leader of the Move Forward Party. Critics (including myself) have suggested that the unchecked power of the Court goes beyond overreach into a sort of rolling judicial coup. Of course, when it was Prayut’s power that was in question – in particular, the question of how long he was able to remain in power – the Court took the middle ground and allowed him to extend his term beyond eight years.
The worst outcome may still lie ahead. While there has been optimism that this year’s general election greenlit conversations about the prospect of a new Constitution, it was a 2025 ruling by this Constitutional Court that required three separate referenda on a new charter, making a smooth transition less likely. In the forthcoming discussions on potential drafts, there is no guarantee that the institutions of old will be removed and replaced with more transparent, accountable ones.
As Hamlet once said, “Aye, there’s the rub.”

articles.title: Vietnam, Canada Announce Establishment of Strategic Partnership
articles.full_text:
As middle powers reliant on international order that is in a state of disarray, Hanoi and Ottawa believe they have a lot to gain from deeper collaboration.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Vietnam’s President To Lam shake hands during their meeting in Ottawa, Canada, Sep. 24, 2026.
Vietnam has elevated its relationship to a Strategic Partnership, as Hanoi’s top leader To Lam paid a state visit to the country – the first ever by a general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV).
During a meeting yesterday in Ottawa, Lam and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the two nations were upgrading the Comprehensive Partnership established in 2017.
Vietnamese state media reported that the two nations “agreed that Vietnam–Canada relations have met all the conditions to enter a new stage of development, characterized by a higher level of political trust, broader and more substantive cooperation, and more closely intertwined interests.”
In a joint statement issued after the meeting, the two sides described themselves as “trusted partners” who were committed to a relationship “grounded in mutual respect for each other’s political system, independence, and sovereignty and territorial integrity” and characterized by “balanced and intertwined interests.”
Although the statement did not use the term, it also referenced their common status as “middle powers” reliant on an international order that is beginning to break down under the pressure of economic protectionism and intensifying geopolitical competition. “As countries with deep integration in the global trading system,” it stated, “Canada and Viet Nam recognize that prosperity depends on rules-based international economic engagements.”
According to the joint statement, the Strategic Partnership is focused on eight primary “pillars” of cooperation: bilateral, regional, and multilateral cooperation; trade and investment; transport and infrastructure; digital technologies and artificial intelligence; energy security; food security; defense and security; and education, culture, and “people-to-people ties.”
It said that these eight pillars “position Canada and Viet Nam to address shared challenges, seize emerging opportunities, and contribute to a more secure, prosperous, and dynamic Indo-Pacific region.”
For Canada, the upgrade to its relationship with Vietnam is consistent with both its recent engagement with Asia and the thrust of the now-famous speech that Carney delivered at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. During the speech, the Canadian leader cited the “rupture” in the world order, and the need for middle powers to “build a new order that encompasses our values, such as respect for human rights, sustainable development, solidarity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the various states.”
Despite their very different political systems, Vietnam and Canada have a lot in common that predicts a future of potentially fruitful cooperation. Both are middle powers bordering two much more powerful countries – China and the United States – that are locked into an increasingly adversarial relationship.
Trade between the two nations has also increased considerably in recent years, reaching $20.6 billion in two-way trade 2025. Vietnam is now Canada’s largest trading partner in ASEAN, while Canada is Vietnam’s ninth-largest in total. Both are also members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, the free trade pact that was negotiated by the U.S. before President Donald Trump withdrew from the agreement in 2017.
For Vietnam, better relations with Canada is a valuable complement to its omnidirectional foreign policy, which seeks to maintain good relations with key partners among both the West and the “rest.” In the two years since taking over as CPV chief, Lam, who was also appointed state president earlier this year, has been particularly energetic in this regard, elevating eight nations into Vietnam’s circle of Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships, the top tier in its diplomatic hierarchy.
In addition to Canada, Vietnam under Lam’s leadership has also established Strategic Partnerships with Czechia, Finland, Bulgaria, and Belarus.

articles.title: Cambodian Authorities Investigating Scamming Sites Linked to Sanctioned Tycoons, Senior Official Says
articles.full_text:
Phnom Penh is trying to address criticisms that the current anti-scam campaign is more about reputation management than full accountability.
Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet addresses the International Conference on Combating Online Scams in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Sep. 23, 2026.
Online scamming sites linked to two sanctioned Cambodian tycoons are among those being investigated by the Cambodian authorities, a senior official said yesterday, as the country concluded a two-day anti-scam conference.
In an interview with Nikkei Asia, Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the government’s ad hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, said that compounds linked to the businessmen Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are being investigated as part of the government’s ongoing anti-scam crackdown.
“For those two tycoons who have compounds that are linked to scams, they are being investigated,” Sinarith said, referring to the properties.
Asked for details of the investigations, Sinarith said that “investigations were ongoing at all suspect compounds and that investigators were still determining the complicity of individuals linked to locations allegedly used for online scams,” in Nikkei’s paraphrase.
As Nikkei’s correspondent Ananth Baliga noted, Sinarith’s comments mark “the first time the government has admitted such well-connected people are associated with investigations into scam operations.”
Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are not minor figures. Both were important allies and financial buttresses of Prime Minister Hun Sen during his 38-year rule, and have remained prominent figures under his son, Hun Manet, who took over the prime ministership in 2023. Both control corporate empires based in (although not confined to) the western provinces of Koh Kong and Banteay Meanchey, respectively, and are also long-serving senators for the Cambodian People’s Party.
Sinarith’s comments came on the second day of the two-day International Conference on Combating Online Scams, which the Cambodian government hosted in Phnom Penh this week.
The conference, which was co-sponsored by Interpol, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime, and China’s Lancang Mekong Cooperation mechanism, was intended to promote global collaboration in the fight against cyber-scams. It also marked the culmination of an anti-scam campaign that Cambodia’s government launched last year, in response to rising pressure from foreign governments, including the United States and China, over the industrial-scale scamming operations that were operating, with apparent impunity, across the country.
Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are among the group of politicians and prominent businesspeople who are alleged to have abetted and/or profited from this wave of cyber-criminality. Both are alleged to own properties where thousands of trafficked workers were held in prison-like conditions by criminal syndicates and were forced to run scams on victims across the globe.
In addition to the independent media reporting alleging such connections, Ly Yong Phat was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department in 2024 for his role “in serious human rights abuse related to the treatment of trafficked workers subjected to forced labor in online scam centers.”
Kok An followed him onto Treasury’s Specially Designated Nationals list in April of this year, when Treasury claimed that he had used his “political connections” to protect a network of scam operations that have “stolen millions of dollars from U.S. victims” through “digital asset investment fraud and other scams.”
Authorities in Thailand have also investigated both tycoons for their ties to online scamming syndicates and money laundering. They have denied any connection to cyber-scam operations.
However, while the Cambodian government’s current crackdown has resulted in the shuttering of dozens of scam compounds and the deportation of tens of thousands of foreign nationals, there have been no signs that it will investigate the allegations against well-connected individuals.
Indeed, the government has defended Ly Yong Phat and Kok An from claims of their involvement in criminal activity, particularly those made by authorities in Thailand, whom they accused of weaponizing the investigations in the context of last year’s border conflict. In 2024, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs described the U.S. sanctions against Ly Yong Phat as “politically motivated.”
Critics of the crackdown say that this is evidence that the current crackdown is a reputation-management exercise rather than a genuine attempt to hold protected figures to account, let alone to alter the political economy that gave Chinese scamming syndicates such a foothold in Cambodia in the first place.
With his comments to Nikkei, Sinarith was clearly trying to address these sorts of concerns – and perhaps to initiate a campaign to have the two businessmen removed from the U.S. sanctions list. However, saying that the compounds allegedly owned by or connected to Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are the subject of investigation does not automatically mean that there will be a full accounting of their alleged role.
Based on several decades of precedent, the likelihood is that these investigations will peter out once the world’s attention has moved on.
