articles.title: Delivered to the Wrong Address? F-35 Parts Re-routed to Hong Kong
articles.full_text:
The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product.
A U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II, assigned to the 158th Fighter Wing, takes off from Burlington International Airport in South Burlington, Vermont, March 11, 2026.
Last summer a shipment of F-35 parts was reportedly re-routed to Hong Kong from its intended destination in Australia. Australia is a partner in the F-35 program; the People’s Republic of China is not. U.S. authorities are reportedly trying to recover the parts and prevent future breaches. The incident has caused consternation in the United States and Australia, both of which have effectively committed to the F-35 as the foundation of their future airpower. And yet the mis-shipment has made clear a fundamental contradiction at the heart of the F-35 project; high tech proprietary classification does not go well with an aggressive policy of export and offshoring. 
In short, it’s hard to keep aspects of the F-35 secret when the United States is aggressively trying to sell the aircraft abroad. 
We do not yet fully understand whether this was an innocent (if catastrophic) error, or if it was the result of a complex and successful Chinese espionage operation. If the latter, we don’t know if Chinese intelligence has been able to exploit the shipment, though it appears that Beijing is in possession of the errant parts. But even if the diversion of the shipment to Hong Kong was accidental and not part of an espionage operation, the incident highlights some of the contradictions inherent in the F-35 program.
The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product that the United States has been trying to aggressively export over the past two decades to most every country in the Global North and a few in the Global South. Jonathan Caverley has called the F-35 “America’s Belt and Road,” because of both its substantial expense and because of its integrated production over several countries and integrated maintenance over several more. Work in all of these countries is spread among dozens of contractors and subcontractors, each of which offers a potential weak link in terms of keeping the parts of the aircraft secret and secure. 
There are a limited number of countries that could usefully exploit the technology in the shipment, and China is one of them. Of particular concern is the canopy, which represents an enormous technological and financial investment and which could conceivably benefit China’s aerospace industry. As with most such cases, the issue here is less that Chinese engineers could copy the equipment and then integrate it into their own aircraft (modern industrial aerospace techniques are remarkably complex) but rather that careful study could reveal vulnerabilities or characteristics that could eventually give Chinese pilots a tactical advantage. 
It’s worth noting that the F-35 is no longer a youthful aircraft. It has been in active service for more than a decade, flies for 12 different countries (and often for more than one air force per country), and boasts some 1,200 operational units across the world. It has flown in combat for Israel and the United States in several wars. Given this record, there’s only so much that can be done to keep the details of the aircraft’s manufacture and performance secret from China or Russia. China has its own fifth-generation fighters and has already worked out many of the problems associated with the critical technologies. Indeed, both China and the United States have moved onto sixth-generation programs. Thus, the availability of the canopy of the F-35 may be important, but it’s hardly critical. articles.title: Burmese Refugees in Thailand Face Fresh Deportation Threat
articles.full_text:
A recently-passed law increases the risk that people fleeing repression will be deported and forcibly recruited into the military’s units of “one-way troops.”
Nway, a Burmese political activist who fled Myanmar to avoid forcible conscription into the military, sits for an interview in Chiang Mai, Thailand, September 2026.
In April of 2026, 23-year-old Nway became scared of the dark for the first time in her life. She would lie awake at night, jumping at the noise of a car engine humming past the house she shared with her single mother, anxious that she could be dragged from her bed as she slept.
Her fear of the dark was not unfounded. As a Burmese political activist who had spent the last four years of her life in prison until April of this year, she was a high-profile target for forced conscription into the Myanmar military, which seized power in a coup in 2021. The military, which now fully controls only around 20 percent of the country’s territory, has conscripted over 30,000 young people since February 2024 in a bid to strengthen their struggling forces.
Since then, young people have been grabbed from the street, their workplaces, and their homes, after which they are reportedly deployed to the frontlines and used as “cannon fodder and human shields.” Nway said that her cousin was abducted by the authorities while drinking with friends by the river in Yangon one evening in 2024. He returned home earlier this year to share that “everyone except him had died; he was the one and only lucky man.”
Nway’s previous activism meant that when she was released from prison, she was targeted by the police, who would sit outside her home and visit her mother weekly to tell her, “if you don’t give us money, she will be listed.” Concerned for her daughter’s safety, Nway’s mother instead paid the authorities for her to fly safely to Thailand. Nway found a community of Burmese refugees and activists in the northern city of Chiang Mai, many of whom had similarly been targeted for conscription before fleeing the country.
Since the military coup, thousands of young refugees like Nway have started to rebuild their lives in Thailand, following in the footsteps of past generations of refugees and exiles. But harassment and arrests from Thai police and a deportation law approved in August continue to threaten their security. The new legal framework has been developed for “administering deportation issues speedily and effectively” in the absence of pre-existing “concrete guidelines.” According to civil society organizations, the new laws are already a source of concern for refugees in Thailand.
When Nway arrived in northern Thailand, she was reunited with Pho Thar, another activist and photojournalist whom she had known at university. Both had been held in separate facilities in Yangon’s Insein Prison for years, reuniting only once they had left the country. Pho Thar has already secured his migrant worker’s card, known as a “pink card,” which is the most accessible way for Myanmar nationals to gain legal residency, and Nway is in the process of securing her own.
Nway and Pho Thar are comfortable sharing their stories and names because they know they can never return to Myanmar. For Nway, this is because an outstanding legal case ensures she will be arrested and likely conscripted. Pho Thar, who has already been arrested four times by the Burmese authorities, believes he will be killed if he returns. Sitting outside a Burmese-owned restaurant on the edge of the city, he cracks his shoulder, a permanent injury sustained during his last arrest.
When Pho Thar was released from prison in November 2025, he knew he was listed for conscription and left Yangon within five days, travelling to Karen State where friends in the People’s Defense Forces helped him cross the border.
Pho Thar decided to travel straight to Chiang Mai when he entered Thailand because he believed the risk of staying in the border city of Mae Sot without documentation would be too high. Almost half of the nearly 4 million Myanmar nationals living in Thailand are undocumented and they face regular harassment, extortion, and threats of deportation from the Thai authorities. A 2025 report by Human Rights Watch (HRW) identified that police bribes had become so prevalent in Mae Sot that they referred to Myanmar nationals as “walking ATMs.”
Fear of the authorities and deportation has ruled the lives of several young Burmese refugees who agreed to speak to The Diplomat on condition of anonymity.
One 22-year-old Burmese refugee, Aung*, said that as an undocumented migrant, he found work in a garment factory where he is paid only 150 baht a day – the equivalent of around $4.50 and below minimum wage – and receives one day off per month. Despite his exhaustion, he is grateful for the layer of protection this workplace provides from the police. “I’m always afraid of the Thai police so I rarely go out to the town, I always stay in my factory,” he said.
In Myanmar, the parents of young people who have fled the country continue to pay bribes to Burmese authorities so their other children are not conscripted instead. Aung said that until August 2026, his mother continued to pay for him. “If I was deported to Myanmar, I would be taken to the frontlines and I will never go back home,” he said. “I face difficulty in Mae Sot so I always miss my home. I want to go back, but it is not possible.”
Thirty-five-year-old music producer Kyaw* also said that his mother, who recently recovered from breast cancer, continues to pay monthly bribes for her three children who have fled the country. He is still waiting for his documents in Mae Sot, and similarly knows that if he was deported he would be forced to join what he calls the “one-way troops” that are sent to the frontlines. He decided to leave Yangon when he went to the smoking area near his workplace and witnessed several young colleagues being kidnapped by military personnel during a work break.
Having already paid a 14-million-kyat bribe – over $6,600 – after being arbitrarily arrested and threatened with conscription, Kyaw started the long journey to the border. “I didn’t want to serve in the military because it’s just a civil war,” he said. “Since moving to Thailand, I have to start from zero but if I don’t have anything to eat I don’t care; I will sing a song for the revolution.”
Elsa, who fled to Mae Sot in 2023 with her family, said that they had to wait until 2025 for them to receive their migrant worker’s cards. She reported that they did not leave their home for four months between April and August in 2024 due to increased patrols and arrests by the authorities. She now works in an office but said that “it is a difficult life.”
Since Thai immigration laws do not recognize Myanmar nationals as refugees, and Thailand has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention, the paths to residency are limited and refugees rely on a broker to navigate the application process for a worker’s card. Interviewees in HRW’s report confirmed that it was unclear exactly what the fees they were paying brokers were being used for in the application process.
In late August, new deportation regulations were approved by the Thai government, which facilitate the prompt deportation of “undesirable” foreigners. Civil society organizations have criticized this legislation, calling for it to include safeguards protecting refugees from deportation. As it stands, while the legislation acknowledges decisions around deportation should account for Thailand’s “relevant international obligations” there is no mention of non-refoulement, which would prevent refugees or asylum seekers from being sent back to any country where they could face persecution or serious harm.
Two foreign nationals have already been deported under the new legal framework. Thanida Piyachot, a human rights specialist at the advocacy group Fortify Rights, said that “the Thai government’s enactment of regulations that can directly affect people’s rights without a thorough review is already deeply concerning. Now, with the enforcement of this fast-track deportation process, serious questions remain about how decisions will be made in practice when there are no clear standards of safeguards.”
Tanyakorn Thippayapokin, the policy, advocacy, and communications coordinator at Asylum Access Thailand, added that it’s very likely the law will be used to extort, harass, and deport Burmese nationals because it is written “very broadly to target anyone staying illegally in the country.”
The Coalition for the Rights of Refugees and Stateless Persons, which includes Fortify Rights and Asylum Access, has called for the government to promptly review the regulations with civil society organizations to address gaps that could put refugees at risk of forced returns and have a standard operating procedure that aligns with principles of non-refoulement.
For the undocumented refugees who are waiting for their migrant worker’s card applications to be processed, this law adds to their concerns about being deported to Myanmar and forcibly recruited. Everyone interviewed by The Diplomat believed that deportation would result in them being conscripted against their will and likely dying on the frontlines, a risk that does not appear to have been considered under this new legal framework, according to civil society organizations.
Piyachot argued that the new law is already impacting the security of undocumented Burmese migrants. “It is creating fear among refugee communities. I believe [the authorities] can use this law to threaten them, and worsen the corruption and extortion,” she said.
Meanwhile, Nway is trying to start a new life in Chiang Mai, alongside Pho Thar. Now she is in Thailand, she says she “doesn’t expect a lot. I really want to go back to my country because it’s where my childhood memories are, but it’s impossible.”
Instead, she says she wants a simple life. “I don’t want to worry again about what will happen at night, like in Yangon,” Nway said. “I want to sleep peacefully.”
*Some names have been changed to preserve respondents’ anonymity.
In April of 2026, 23-year-old Nway became scared of the dark for the first time in her life. She would lie awake at night, jumping at the noise of a car engine humming past the house she shared with her single mother, anxious that she could be dragged from her bed as she slept.
Her fear of the dark was not unfounded. As a Burmese political activist who had spent the last four years of her life in prison until April of this year, she was a high-profile target for forced conscription into the Myanmar military, which seized power in a coup in 2021. The military, which now fully controls only around 20 percent of the country’s territory, has conscripted over 30,000 young people since February 2024 in a bid to strengthen their struggling forces.
Since then, young people have been grabbed from the street, their workplaces, and their homes, after which they are reportedly deployed to the frontlines and used as “cannon fodder and human shields.” Nway said that her cousin was abducted by the authorities while drinking with friends by the river in Yangon one evening in 2024. He returned home earlier this year to share that “everyone except him had died; he was the one and only lucky man.”
articles.summary: A recently-passed law increases the risk that people fleeing repression will be deported and forcibly recruited into the military’s units of "one-way troops."

articles.title: 166 Civil Society Groups Urge Halt to Malaysia’s Rohingya Deportation Plan
articles.full_text:
The organizations expressed “grave concern” about the repatriation of refugees to Myanmar, citing the risks of violent persecution and forced conscription.
Two elderly Rohingya refugees at their home in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
More than 160 civil society organizations yesterday urged Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to halt plans to deport ​Rohingya refugees to Myanmar, saying that they could face severe risks including ongoing violence ‌and forced conscription into the military.
Last week, Anwar said that he planned to invite military-appointed leader Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia, in a bid to expedite the repatriation of tens of thousands of Rohingya Muslims who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia over the past decade.
Anwar’s government has already reached a deal with Naypyidaw for the “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 refugees, which make up around half of the 10,388 Myanmar nationals currently being held at the country’s immigration detention depots. The first 1,476 of this group is scheduled to return to Myanmar on September 29 aboard two Myanmar Navy warships and a hospital ship.
In their statement, the civil society groups, which included both Malaysian, Myanmar, and international organizations, expressed “grave concern” about the planned deportations, contrasting Malaysia’s treatment of the Rohingya with its vocal advocacy of the Palestinian cause. They also lambasted Anwar’s willingness to roll out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing.
“Malaysia’s engagement with the junta must not come at the expense of its own reputation and integrity. Cozying up to genocidaires while criminalizing their survivors is not only illogical but also immoral,” the groups said. “Refoulement of the Rohingya by Malaysia or any ASEAN member state will make them complicit in the ongoing genocide of the Rohingya.”
In their statement, the civil society groups pointed to the continuing conflict in Rakhine State, the home of most Rohingya refugees. It also pointed to a pattern of forced conscription of Rohingya populations by the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist armed group that now controls the majority of Rakhine.
The groups called for an “immediate halt” to the planned deportations of all Myanmar nationals, pending a “comprehensive assessment of the situation” in the country.
“Sending Rohingya into a situation of forced conscription will prolong and intensify rather than reduce the conflict,” it stated.
Large numbers of Rohingya have flowed into Malaysian since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. As of February, 193,800 refugees from Myanmar were registered with the U.N. refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, of which 126,000 were Rohingya. Malaysia does not recognize any of them as refugees.
In recent months, Anwar has come under growing pressure to respond a tide of public hostility toward the Rohingya in Malaysia, which has been marked by an upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric, particularly online, and inflammatory comments by prominent public figures, who have described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country. Across the country, Rohingya refugee schools ​have been forced to close due to harassment and ⁠threats.

But the growing domestic pressure over refugees has forced Anwar to adopt a more accommodating position toward Naypyidaw.
In a podcast interview last week, he announced plans to invite Min Aung Hlaing to undertake an official visit to Malaysia, which would make it the fifth ASEAN member state to welcome the coup leader since he was elected president by Myanmar’s military-dominated parliament in April. Anwar said that Malaysia was not ready to recognize the government, ⁠but needed an authority to negotiate with on returning refugees.
“I invited him to say we can be friends, ​we can trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them [the refugees] back,” he said. “Otherwise, this will continue to place a burden on security, and the economy, while also creating tensions among the public.”
This language was echoed by the Ministry of Home Affairs in its announcement of the September 29 deportation, when it said that the refugees’ presence had become a “major financial burden, caused serious social problems, and created a real security threat to the country.”

articles.title: Rare Earths at the Trump-Xi Summit: Relief Without a Resolution
articles.full_text:
The Trump-Xi meeting may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.
Rare earths entered the Trump-Xi summit before the two leaders even sat down. On September 21, two days before President Xi Jinping’s arrival in the United States, China’s Foreign Ministry faced a series of questions on whether Beijing had “fully resumed rare earth deliveries,” whether a “November 10 deadline or expanded restrictions on rare earth exports” could be extended, and whether rare earths controls involving Japan would feature in the Washington talks. The responses were deliberately cautious: Beijing reiterated its commitment to “keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable,” but emphasized that dual-use exports would remain subject to legal and security considerations. 
The Foreign Ministry’s responses captured the central paradox of the summit: it may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.
In April 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs placed several medium and heavy rare earth elements – including samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium – under export controls. Exporters of these items are required to apply for licenses, with the stated legal basis including China’s Export Control Law and regulations on dual-use items. This does not amount to a blanket ban on exports, but it does shift rare earth access from a purely commercial transaction to a regulated process shaped by licensing, end-use review, and national security considerations. Once such controls are embedded in a legal and bureaucratic system, they are not easily removed. A summit can improve predictability, but it will not result in the dismantling of China’s carefully built legal framework for export controls.
The same logic applies on the U.S. side. Even if the summit reduces short-term pressure, Washington is unlikely to abandon its effort to diversify away from China-centered critical mineral supply chains. In January 2026, the White House framed U.S. dependence on imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products as a national security concern, noting that even where the United States has domestic mining capacity, it often lacks sufficient downstream processing capacity. The policy response has therefore gone beyond asking China for more predictable deliveries. The United States is investing in domestic processing, recycling and alternative supply chains, while also working with allies and partners to reduce exposure to single-source dependence. In this sense, any relief produced by the summit may buy some time, but it will not weaken Washington’s broader push for supply-chain diversification.
Rare earths occupy this strategic space because they are not simply another category of traded minerals. Their importance lies less in the raw materials themselves than in the capabilities of the downstream industries they support: high-performance magnets, electric vehicles, wind turbines, advanced electronics and defense systems. This gives rare earths a dual character. They are commercial inputs for global industries, but they are also strategic enablers for military and technological power. 
Once a commodity acquires this dual-use profile, access to it is unlikely to be governed by market logic alone. For China, this strengthens the case for licensing and end-use scrutiny. For the United States, it reinforces the argument that dependence on China-centered supply chains is not merely an economic risk, but a strategic vulnerability. Rare earths can be discussed at the summit but the underlying strategic issues are not easily resolved.
This creates an asymmetric form of interdependence. China does not control every part of the global rare earth supply chain, but its position in processing and export licensing gives it a more immediate ability to shape access. The United States is not without options, but its alternatives require time: new processing capacity must be built, recycling systems expanded, and supply arrangements with allies and partners made commercially viable. This mismatch between China’s immediate leverage and the United States’ long-term adjustment capacity creates bargaining space, but not enough for a full reset. The result is a prolonged period of managed vulnerability on rare earths.
Where the summit could still matter lies in the management of risk. Neither side benefits from an uncontrolled shock to the rare earths market. China wants to preserve its right to screen sensitive exports, but it also has an interest in presenting itself as a stable supplier of critical minerals. The United States, meanwhile, wants to reduce dependence on China-centered supply chains, but it also needs time to build alternatives. This creates room for limited accommodation: clearer licensing procedures, smoother civilian trade, and more regular communication over end-use concerns. Yet these would be instruments of crisis management rather than signs of strategic convergence. The summit may reduce uncertainty over how the rules are applied, but it is unlikely to change the rules themselves. 
The Trump-Xi summit, therefore, should not be read as a turning point in rare earth politics. Its significance lies less in changing the direction of policy than in clarifying the limits of what diplomacy can achieve. For Beijing, rare earths will remain a strategic resource subject to state control. For Washington, any temporary easing will not remove the underlying concern that dependence on China-centered supply chains creates long-term strategic exposure.
This is the meaning of relief without a resolution. In the emerging logic of China-U.S. geoeconomic competition, critical minerals are instruments of leverage, symbols of vulnerability, and test of strategic resilience.

articles.title: Will the World Ever Take Action on Myanmar?
articles.full_text:
The evidence of atrocities is there. What are governments prepared to do with that knowledge?
The Human Rights and Alliance of Civilizations Room at the United Nations’ Geneva headquarters, which houses the United Nations Human Rights Council.
We came to Geneva for the 63rd Human Rights Council from different points in our advocacy journeys and different parts of the world, but with a shared commitment to the people of Myanmar. One of us has spent years walking the corridors of the United Nations, meeting diplomats, and pressing governments to act on the crisis in Myanmar. The other was attending the Human Rights Council for the first time, after years of documenting human rights violations in the country.
We were there for the same reason: to ask governments what they are prepared to do about Myanmar. After years of documenting atrocities, we left Geneva with a question that is becoming increasingly difficult to avoid: what happens when the evidence is already there?
Inside the Human Rights Council chamber, the scale of the crisis was once again laid bare.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, described a deepening crisis marked by attacks by the military junta, including airstrikes, forced conscription, arbitrary detention, sexual violence, displacement, and the weaponization of humanitarian assistance. He urged United Nations member states to refer the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court through the Security Council and halt transfers of arms, ammunition, jet fuel, and dual-use items that risk facilitating violations of international law.
The head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, Nicholas Koumjian, reported that serious international crimes are being committed with greater frequency and intensity. The mechanism is continuing to collect and preserve evidence for future accountability.
At HRC63, we heard a wide range of approaches to the crisis in Myanmar.
Of the 39 governments and entities that took the floor, fewer than half – just 14 – explicitly raised accountability, justice, impunity, or international accountability mechanisms. While 20 speakers expressed broad support for stronger action, the rest of the room fragmented: eight, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, India, and Vietnam, appeared supportive but cautious, favoring regional engagement, dialogue, and a “Myanmar-owned or Myanmar-led” process.
Five governments – Laos, Belarus, Russia, China, and Venezuela – actively shielded the regime, emphasizing sovereignty, non-interference, and engagement with Myanmar’s authorities, while opposing international pressure.
After the session, we met with several diplomatic missions in Geneva. For us, these meetings created space for conversations about what more can be done. What we heard in the Council and in those meetings was not a lack of awareness. Myanmar is simply not a sufficiently high political priority for many governments to generate sustained action.
There are real diplomatic complications. Myanmar’s political representation remains contested, including at the United Nations, where the question of who represents the country remains unresolved. Governments also have different relationships with the military junta, the National Unity Government, ethnic resistance organizations, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). But these complications cannot be grounds for indefinite inaction and impunity.
In our view, a Myanmar-led or ASEAN-led process should have a major role. Humanitarian assistance is essential. But none of these should mean putting accountability or the protection of civilians on hold.
Dialogue with a brutal regime cannot become a substitute for accountability, and sovereignty cannot serve as a shield against international scrutiny.
Human rights defenders, within Myanmar and outside, are still doing their part. We continue to document violations, speak with survivors, share evidence with the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, and engage with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Other Myanmar and regional organizations are doing the same.
Fortify Rights has documented the military’s aerial attacks on civilians, including the chain of command behind attacks in Kachin and Karenni states, and has continued to record new methods of aerial warfare.
Although more documentation is needed, what is missing is a comparable machinery of political action. 
Some governments are already using some of the tools available to them. Canada maintains an arms embargo and aviation-fuel prohibition and has continued imposing targeted sanctions on Myanmar military officials and entities. The United Kingdom and the European Union have also imposed sanctions targeting aviation fuel suppliers and other entities linked to the military. 
At the same time, accountability efforts are moving forward. Myanmar and Rohingya organizations have pursued universal-jurisdiction cases in Argentina, Germany, Indonesia, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, and Turkiye. In November 2024, the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, while in January 2026, the International Court of Justice held merits hearings in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar.
And yet, from where we sit, there is still a striking gap between the evidence being gathered and meaningful accountability for crimes committed since the 2021 coup. No international court is currently prosecuting the full range of those crimes. National cases and international proceedings offer important pathways, but they do not yet amount to a comprehensive accountability process.
What stayed with us from the 63rd Human Rights Council was not a lack of information or evidence. The evidence is being collected, and governments should continue to fund human rights documentation. Cases are being pursued. Some governments are taking action. But the pieces are still not coming together at the scale needed to match the crisis.
We can continue to document, share evidence, and engage governments. But documentation can only go so far without political action. The people of Myanmar have been waiting for years, and the evidence is there. What happens next depends on what governments do with it.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, described a deepening crisis marked by attacks by the military junta, including airstrikes, forced conscription, arbitrary detention, sexual violence, displacement, and the weaponization of humanitarian assistance. He urged United Nations member states to refer the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court through the Security Council and halt transfers of arms, ammunition, jet fuel, and dual-use items that risk facilitating violations of international law.
The head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, Nicholas Koumjian, reported that serious international crimes are being committed with greater frequency and intensity. The mechanism is continuing to collect and preserve evidence for future accountability.
At HRC63, we heard a wide range of approaches to the crisis in Myanmar.
Of the 39 governments and entities that took the floor, fewer than half – just 14 – explicitly raised accountability, justice, impunity, or international accountability mechanisms. While 20 speakers expressed broad support for stronger action, the rest of the room fragmented: eight, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, India, and Vietnam, appeared supportive but cautious, favoring regional engagement, dialogue, and a “Myanmar-owned or Myanmar-led” process.
Five governments – Laos, Belarus, Russia, China, and Venezuela – actively shielded the regime, emphasizing sovereignty, non-interference, and engagement with Myanmar’s authorities, while opposing international pressure.
articles.summary: The evidence of atrocities is there. What are governments prepared to do with that knowledge?

articles.title: Xi Jinping Is Coming to the US. Why Is He Skipping the UNGA?
articles.full_text:
Xi’s coming to the U.S. East Coast while the United Nations’ biggest event is going on. That makes his absence all the more striking.
Chinese President Xi Jinping addresses the general debate of the General Assembly’s 70th session, Sep. 28, 2015. That was the first and only time Xi attended a session of the UNGA in person.
If you read The Diplomat, you probably follow Asia-Pacific affairs – and thus you probably already know that Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington, D.C. today for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.
According to the White House’s itinerary, Xi will land at Andrews Air Force Base on September 23, where he will be personally received by Trump himself. The next day, he’ll receive a formal welcome ceremony at the White House, followed by the actual summit and a state dinner. On September 25, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife for tea; both couples will then visit the National Archives, “where they will view a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history.” Then Xi and his delegation will fly home.
What’s most remarkable about this itinerary is what it doesn’t include: a stop in New York, where the United Nations’ General Assembly is currently holding its 81st session. Heads of state and government from around the world are making the trip to New York just for the UNGA, including top leaders from Bangladesh, Japan, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Mongolia, South Korea, and Vietnam, just to name a few from The Diplomat’s coverage region.
Meanwhile, Xi is making a trip across the Pacific Ocean and the entire continental U.S. and not bothering to take an extra jaunt up the coast to attend the United Nations’ most important annual event.
Instead, Vice President Han Zheng will be in New York from September 24 to 26 to represent China at the UNGA. According to China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, “On the sidelines of the general debate, Vice President Han will attend the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with [the] U.N. secretary-general, president of the 81st UNGA session, and leaders of relevant countries.”
Apparently, these are meetings Xi couldn’t be bothered to attend himself, despite being just an hour’s plane ride away. 
Xi’s absence from the UNGA would seem to undermine China’s consistent rhetorical emphasis on the United Nations’ importance. China’s white paper on global governance, released in June 2026, repeatedly emphasized the U.N. as the “core” of the international  order. “The United Nations is the primary platform for practicing multilateralism and advancing global governance,” the white paper declared. “Its leading position must be upheld and remain rock solid; its role can only be reinforced, not weakened.”
In the same press conference where Guo announced Han’s trip, the spokesperson repeated a similar line: “The United Nations is the core platform for global governance, and the general debate of UNGA is a vital opportunity for countries to build political consensus and coordinate multilateral actions.” But if the United Nations, and the UNGA, are so important, why can’t Xi be bothered to attend?
Xi has gone to the UNGA just once since becoming China’s top leader in late 2012. He went in 2015, to commemorate the United Nations’ 70th anniversary, and addressed the UNGA in person for the first and only time.
Notably, this coincided with Xi’s last state visit to the United States, when he included attendance at the UNGA within a broader itinerary that saw him also hold a summit with then-U.S. President Barack Obama. That makes the decision not to do the same thing in 2026 all the more notable.
In 2021, Xi gave a video address to the UNGA, in which he announced China’s Global Development Initiative. He has not delivered a speech before the UNGA since.
Perhaps most notably, Xi chose to skip last year’s UNGA – the 80th session. China puts much stock in these round-number anniversaries, pegging trips abroad and major upgrades in bilateral relations to special dates. Remember that Xi took the time to attend the United Nations’ 70th anniversary in person. That wasn’t an aberration – China’s top leader had attended every decennial anniversary of the U.N. since Jiang Zemin in 1995. That made Xi’s absence from the 80th anniversary in 2025 all the more conspicuous. 
Instead [of attending the UNGA], Xi stayed in China, where he “extended festive greetings” for the farmers’ harvest celebration and visited Urumqi to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
Those events were duly splashed across the front-page headlines of People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party. Premier Li Qiang’s presence at UNGA received just a one-line mention on the front page for September 24.
Xi has also stopped announcing China’s major global initiatives at the United Nations. He unveiled the Global Development Initiative at the UNGA back in 2021, albeit in a virtual speech. But in 2025, Xi chose to announce the new Global Governance Initiative – even more directly related to the United Nations’ mission – at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit held in China a month before the UNGA.
Similarly, China founded its own World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) – “an independent intergovernmental international organization that… aims to promote international cooperation and global governance on artificial intelligence” – rather than working within the United Nations to legitimize its efforts toward the same ends. China announced WAICO at its own AI conference, rather than at the U.N. Global Dialogue on AI Governance held a month earlier.
Meanwhile, as Trump reduces U.S. funding for the United Nations, China hasn’t stepped up to fill the gap. Its own U.N.-assessed contributions have been chronically late and remain a mere fraction of what the United States was contributing prior to Trump taking office.
No matter the lip service China pays to the United Nations’ “core role” in global governance, Beijing clearly prefers to give attention, money, and prestige to settings where it exerts more control. That includes China-led groups like the SCO, but also purely bilateral meetings like the summit with Trump. 
Nikkei Asia theorized that Xi’s decision to skip the UNGA was an attempt to position China as a true equal to the United States – a message that apparently would have been diluted by Xi rubbing elbows with leaders from smaller states in New York. That in itself is telling. For all China’s rhetoric about a multipolar world where all states have equal representation – and equal say – in global governance, when push comes to shove Beijing defaults to a different perspective.
As China’s top diplomat put it, fairly undiplomatically, in a heated ASEAN meeting back in 2010: “China is a big country and other countries are small countries, and that’s just a fact.” One of the perks of being a “big country,” as Trump has repeatedly shown, is the privilege of ignoring the United Nations to pursue national interests in other settings.

articles.title: On Taiwan, US ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Is Not Dead Yet
articles.full_text:
What look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks at a press conference at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, Jan. 3, 2026.
Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.
To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.”  Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.” 
Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.
Trump has repeatedly made four points about Taiwan, all of which call into question a robust U.S. response to military action by Beijing. The first is that Taiwan is vastly smaller and less important than China. Second, he says Taiwan is indefensible – too close to China and far from the United States. Third, Trump thinks Taiwan free-rides on U.S. defense. Finally, he complains about Taiwan allegedly stealing America’s semiconductor industry. Shortly before he took office for the second time, Trump said he would respond to a Chinese invasion of Taiwan with economic sanctions.
On top of this, Trump avoids antagonizing Beijing over the Taiwan issue, presumably to clear the way for a China-U.S. bilateral economic deal. During his keynote speech at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not mention Taiwan, a change from his speech the previous year. The unclassified version of the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy also does not mention Taiwan by name.
After his May 2026 meeting with Xi Jinping, Trump criticized the Taiwan government for allegedly flirting with independence due to the presumption of U.S. support. “[W]e’re not looking to have somebody say, ‘Let’s go independent because the United States is backing us,’” he told Fox News.
For good measure, Trump announced that he was delaying a large arms sale to Taiwan already approved by Congress, calling such sales a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with China. He also dismissed the Six Assurances, part of U.S. policy toward Taiwan since the Reagan era. 
The idea that strategic ambiguity has lost its usefulness, however, is wrong. Despite particular statements by Trump that are adverse to Taiwan, U.S. policy remains broadly supportive of Taipei. 
The Pentagon’s 2026 National Defense Strategy said the United States will “erect” and “sustain a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain.” Even a cursory look at a map indicates that aspiration is meaningless without a U.S. intent to prevent China from absorbing Taiwan. 
The large arms sale is delayed, but not canceled. This latest package of armaments is all business, not symbolic. It includes weapons systems appropriate for the scenario of an attempted amphibious invasion by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA): HIMARS rockets, ATACMS missiles, ALTIUS loitering munition drones, Javelin and TOW anti-tank missiles, and mobile howitzers.
U.S. military transits through the Taiwan Strait continue, albeit about half as often as during Trump’s first term.
U.S. security cooperation with the Philippines and Japan, highly relevant to deterring China from moving aggressively against Taiwan, has deepened during the second Trump administration.
The United States got access to, and set aside funding to develop infrastructure in, additional base sites in the northern Philippines, close to the Taiwan Strait. The annual Balikatan military exercises were larger than ever before in 2025 and 2026 and brought in Japan and Australia. U.S. forces deployed NMESIS and Typhon missile systems to the Philippines. The stridency of China’s complaints about these deployments indicate they present problems for Chinese planners.
Washington’s plan to upgrade U.S. Forces Japan to a joint force combat headquarters has proceeded under Trump’s second administration. U.S. and Japanese armed forces increased their interoperability in 2025 and 2026 through more integrated command-and-control structures, more complex joint exercises, and more sharing of data. The United States started supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Japan. Washington and Tokyo are engaged in serious discussions about Japan producing warships or components for the U.S. Navy to help it close the gap with China’s production. 
Strategic ambiguity still holds because what look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
The stances of the Joe Biden presidency and the second Trump administration are different. Biden said on four occasions that the United States would militarily intervene in a cross-strait war, placing him close to an unambiguous pre-commitment to intervention. Trump is closer to the other end, a pre-commitment to non-intervention.
Both, however, represent forms of strategic ambiguity. One president seemed committed and the other reluctant, but who knows what either of them would actually decide to do at crunch time. Beijing still cannot confidently assume a Trump-led United States would not intervene in a Taiwan scenario despite Trump seemingly indicating reticence to do so.
Chinese analysts consider Trump to be unpredictable. They cannot be sure he will act in a way consistent with his past statements.  The Chinese remember how quickly Trump turned on them in 2020. In January, he said “our relationship with China now might be the best it’s been in a long, long time.” Later in the year, largely over the COVID-19 pandemic, Trump regularly berated China with statements such as “I’m very angry at China” and “The world is now suffering as a result of the malfeasance of the Chinese government.”
There are, nevertheless, reasons to doubt the American commitment to defend Taiwan, and these reasons go beyond the current U.S. presidential administration.
First, the demographic trend in the United States is increasingly anti-war. Gen Z Americans, born 1997-2012, are significantly less fearful of China attaining a stronger global position and less likely to see China as an adversary. The succession of unpopular wars against Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran further strengthens the aversion of Americans toward getting embroiled in foreign conflicts.
Second, the costs and risks of maintaining U.S. strategic pre-eminence on the western Pacific Rim against the determination of China to achieve regional supremacy are rising. The United States already dominates the Western Hemisphere. The rationale for dominating the Asia-Pacific, as well, is that doing so makes war less likely and opens the door for U.S. commerce. This rationale is less persuasive, however, if China supports international trade and if opposing China’s aspirations for “rejuvenation” makes war more rather than less likely.
Military analyst Jennifer Kavanaugh’s September 10 proposal for a “Second Island Chain strategy” attracted much attention. Kavanaugh, a member of the “restrainer” camp in U.S. foreign policy, argued that to reduce the risk of war with China while still protecting the most vital U.S. interests, Washington should end its alliances with Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines, pull most of its military forces out of the region, and announce that it will not intervene to protect Taiwan in a cross-strait war. Expect arguments such as this to grow in volume and frequency.
Finally, the U.S. defense industrial base is currently unable to compete with China’s productivity. This weakness is not easily fixed, even with an increased defense budget. As the modernization of its armed forces have made China a near-peer adversary of the United States, China’s advantage in manufacturing capacity becomes potentially decisive in a theoretical China-U.S. war.  
Recent wargaming suggests both China and the U.S. would suffer huge losses in a conflict. Even where the U.S. “wins,” China is better placed to quickly rebuild and rearm its forces, giving Beijing hope that it would prevail in a second round. If American leaders conclude the math leaves them without a path to victory, they will reconsider whether an intervention is feasible. 
But for now, Beijing would be reckless not to assume that both the United States and Japan would militarily oppose an attempt to conquer Taiwan. And Xi is not reckless.
Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.
To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.”  Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.” 
Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.

articles.title: The Trump-Xi Summit: Stakes for Australia
articles.full_text:
Trump wants more sales. Xi wants fewer constraints. What does Australia need from the Trump-Xi summit?
U.S. President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping before a bilateral meeting at the Gimhae International Airport terminal in Busan, South Korea, Oct. 30, 2025.
Chinese media have confirmed that Xi Jinping will make a state visit to Washington from September 23 to 25 for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump. The announcement followed talks between their economic chiefs in New York on September 20. 
Although the two sides have framed those discussions differently, it is clear that trade and AI will be on the summit agenda. Trump could leave with more orders, Xi with fewer constraints on China’s technological development, and both declare success. For Canberra, the question is what their bargain would mean for Australian investments and security arrangements built around sustained China-U.S. competition.
Allied unease is already visible. On September 21, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Japanese and South Korean counterparts in New York. Their joint statement reiterated the United States’ “ironclad” defence commitments, opposed economic coercion, and stressed peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae secured a meeting with Trump on September 22, just before the summit, while South Korean President Lee Jae-myung sought contact during the United Nations General Assembly. Tokyo and Seoul want their security and economic concerns heard before Trump meets Xi. Canberra should draw the same lesson.
Like the Trump-Xi summit held in Beijing in May, this one is likely to buy time rather than lasting stability. The deadline that matters for business falls around November 10. Three temporary arrangements approach their expiration date: Washington’s suspension of restrictions on majority-owned affiliates of listed entities, China’s suspension of expanded rare earth and related export controls, and 178 U.S. tariff exclusions for Chinese goods. The practical questions are how long these pauses will be extended and on what terms.
Trump wants commercial wins ahead of the midterms. Xi wants fewer constraints on China’s technological development. Trade concessions can serve both purposes without resolving the contest over power in the digital age.
Trade and technology may therefore move in different directions. Tariff relief and purchase commitments could coexist with tighter restrictions on advanced chips and overseas computing access. Xi cannot assume Trump can trade these restrictions away. They have bipartisan support in Congress and deep backing in the Pentagon and Commerce Department. 
Beijing increasingly treats efforts to block its technological advance as a challenge to its right to development, one of the four red lines in Xi’s book. It will resist broader technology restrictions and pressure on third countries to choose sides.
The two leaders have different philosophies of negotiation. Trump assumes that, at the right price, almost any arrangement can be renegotiated. Xi allows for pragmatism and ambiguity within fixed limits. Beijing accepts broadly worded commitments but demands clarity on Taiwan and its political system. Washington insists on verifiable trade commitments while deliberately leaving uncertain whether it would intervene militarily over Taiwan. Both leaders have domestic reasons to compromise, but both may sign the same wording and mean different things.
Australia has to plan for the consequences. Canberra should compare their announcements for differences in scope, duration, and conditions before treating a diplomatic statement as a reliable basis for the future.
The Albanese government has spent years restoring normal trade with China while supporting Washington’s efforts to reduce dependence on it. If Trump and Xi compromise with one another, Australia could be left bearing the costs of reducing dependence on China while Washington negotiates exceptions for itself.
Canberra should seek durable support for mineral projects, cooperation on shared AI risks, and security commitments that survive a bargain with Beijing.
First, critical minerals offer one test. The Australia-U.S. framework envisages price support and financing to develop alternatives to Chinese supply. If Washington and Beijing extend their rare earth arrangements, Canberra should seek assurances that support for Australian alternatives will endure. Australian projects need dependable financing and long-term customers, even when Chinese supplies become easier to obtain.
Second, AI risks extend beyond chips and data centers. Australian businesses use software and digital services shared across borders. Canberra should therefore press for an agreement to warn affected countries and operators of serious AI incidents while there is still time to contain them. Building more local data centers would not, by itself, remove those shared dependencies.
Government hotlines alone cannot do this: the first warning may come from a developer, cloud provider, or independent researcher. Those warnings need to reach Australian authorities and affected businesses without waiting for governments to establish blame. That would give Australia something a bilateral technology deal cannot guarantee: timely notice of a failure that could spread into its own economy. The test is whether warnings reach those who must act, rather than whether the leaders agree to keep talking.
Finally, Australia needs maritime security. Defense-commissioned research reported in 2022 found that a major regional conflict would threaten routes supplying 90 percent of Australia’s refined-fuel imports. With disruption in the Strait of Hormuz already imposing costs, Australia can ill afford another obstructed route in the South China Sea.
Canberra should seek consultation before Washington negotiates any changes affecting its regional military presence or commitments under AUKUS. It should also press for functioning military hotlines and arrangements for reporting incidents at sea and in the air. These mechanisms need procedures both sides will use when tensions rise.
Reaffirming that decisions to use nuclear weapons must remain under human control at the summit would provide another practical safeguard.
Canberra’s test is whether the summit leaves Australia better able to invest, keep essential services running, and protect its trade routes. That requires commitments Washington will honor and crisis arrangements both powers will use. If Trump and Xi buy themselves time while Australia is left carrying the uncertainty, their success will not be ours.
